prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: The variable you change on purpose
A variable you keep the same
A testable prediction, with a reason

hints: The dependent variable *depends* on the one you change.
solution: Independent → you change it. Dependent → you measure it. Controlled → you keep it the same. Hypothesis → a testable prediction with a reason.

prompt: In an experiment, what is the variable you **measure** called?

options.text: The dependent variable
The independent variable
The controlled variable
The hypothesis

feedback.b: The independent variable is the one you change.
feedback.c: Controlled variables are the ones you keep the same.
feedback.d: A hypothesis is a prediction, not a variable.

hints: Its value *depends* on what you changed.
solution: The variable you measure is the **dependent variable**, because its value depends on the independent variable you changed.

prompt: What do we call a test where only one variable is changed and all the others are kept the same?
hints: It's a ____ test.
solution: A **fair test**. Only the independent variable changes, so you know it caused any change in the results.

prompt: Which of these is a **testable** question?

options.text: How does the height of a ramp affect how far a toy car rolls?
Are toy cars more fun than skateboards?
What is the best toy car ever made?
Why do people like fast cars?

feedback.b: "Fun" is an opinion, so you can't measure it.
feedback.c: "Best" is an opinion unless you say what you will measure.
feedback.d: This is about people's opinions, not something you can measure with a fair test.

hints: A testable question links two things you can measure.
solution: "How does the height of a ramp affect how far a toy car rolls?" is testable. You can change the ramp height and **measure** the distance.

prompt: Tama tests how the area of a parachute affects how long it takes to fall to the ground. The independent variable is the [[a]]. The dependent variable is the [[b]].
hints: Which one does Tama choose, and which one does he time with a stopwatch?
solution: Tama **changes** the **area of the parachute** (independent) and **measures** the **time taken to fall** (dependent). The drop height should be kept the same, so it's a controlled variable.

prompt: In Tama's parachute investigation (area of parachute vs time to fall), which of these should be **controlled variables**? Select all that apply.

options.text: The height the parachute is dropped from
The mass hanging under the parachute
The length of the strings
The area of the parachute
The time taken to fall
The material the parachute is made from

hints: Leave out the variable Tama changes and the one he measures.
solution: Controlled: **drop height, hanging mass, string length and material**. The area is the independent variable and the time to fall is the dependent variable.

prompt: Liam wraps three beakers of hot water in different materials (wool, cotton and aluminium foil) and measures how much each one cools in 20 minutes. What type of graph should he draw?

options.text: A bar graph, because the materials are categories
A line graph, because temperature is a number
A pie graph, because there are three materials
A scatter graph with no labels

feedback.b: A line graph needs numbers on **both** axes. The independent variable here (material) is a category.
feedback.c: Pie graphs show parts of a whole, not results from a fair test.
feedback.d: Graphs always need labelled axes, and the materials aren't numbers.

hints: Look at the independent variable. Is it a number or a category?
solution: The independent variable (type of material) is a **category**, so use a **bar graph**. Line graphs are for when both variables are numbers.

prompt: Scientists repeat each test several times and calculate the [[a]]. This makes their results more [[b]].
hints: One bad result has less effect when it is averaged with others.
solution: Repeating and calculating the **mean** (average) makes results more **reliable**, because one-off mistakes have less effect.

prompt: Hana drops a paper helicopter three times. It takes 2.4 s, 2.6 s and 2.5 s to fall. What is the mean time?
hints: Add the three times, then divide by 3.

prompt: What name is given to a result that doesn't fit the pattern of the other results?
hints: It "lies out" away from the others.
solution: An **outlier** (or **anomalous result**). Check it or repeat that test, and leave it out when you calculate the mean.

prompt: Mia is investigating how water temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. Which is the best **hypothesis**?

options.text: If the water is warmer, then the sugar will dissolve faster, because the water particles move faster.
Sugar dissolves in water.
I will put a sugar cube into water at 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C.
The sugar will dissolve.

feedback.b: This is a fact, not a prediction about how one variable affects another.
feedback.c: This is part of the method.
feedback.d: This doesn't say how the temperature affects anything, so it can't be tested.

hints: A hypothesis predicts how the independent variable affects the dependent variable, and gives a reason.
solution: A good hypothesis predicts the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable and gives a reason: **if the water is warmer, the sugar will dissolve faster, because the particles move faster**.

prompt:
Wiremu measures his reaction time by catching a falling ruler. He catches it at 14 cm, 15 cm, 13 cm and 31 cm. On the 4th go he was distracted.

Leave out the outlier and calculate the mean catch distance.
hints: Which result doesn't fit the pattern?
Find the mean of the other three results.
solution: 31 cm is the **outlier**: it's far from the others and has a known cause. Mean of the other three: $\dfrac{14 + 15 + 13}{3} = \dfrac{42}{3} = 14$ cm.

prompt: Put these stages of a science investigation in order.

items.text: Plan a fair test and decide on the variables
Carry out the test and record results in a table
Draw a graph of the results
Write a conclusion and evaluate the method

hints: You need a question before you can predict an answer to it.
You can't graph results you haven't collected yet.
solution: Question → hypothesis → plan (variables, fair test) → carry out and record → graph → conclusion and evaluation.

prompt:
Isla puts an effervescent (fizzy) tablet into water at different temperatures and times how long it fizzes.

| Water temperature (°C) | Time to stop fizzing (s) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 95 |
| 20 | 70 |
| 30 | 52 |
| 40 | 38 |
| 50 | 30 |

Which conclusion is best supported by her results?

options.text: As the water temperature increases, the tablet takes less time to stop fizzing.
As the water temperature increases, the tablet takes more time to stop fizzing.
The water temperature has no effect on the time.
At 60 °C the tablet will stop fizzing after exactly 22 s.

feedback.b: Look again: the times get smaller as the temperature goes up.
feedback.c: The times change a lot, from 95 s down to 30 s.
feedback.d: Her results don't go up to 60 °C, so she can't say "exactly". The pattern is also levelling off.

hints: Read down both columns. As one goes up, what does the other do?
solution: As the temperature rises from 10 °C to 50 °C, the time falls from 95 s to 30 s. So **the warmer the water, the faster the reaction** (the less time it takes).

prompt: Noah times how long a paper helicopter takes to fall 2 m, using a stopwatch. What is the most likely **source of error**?

options.text: His reaction time when starting and stopping the stopwatch
Using the same drop height every time
Making every helicopter from the same type of paper
Writing the results in a table

feedback.b: Keeping the drop height the same is good practice. It's a controlled variable.
feedback.c: Using the same paper is good practice. It's a controlled variable.
feedback.d: Recording results in a table is correct practice, not a source of error.

hints: The fall only takes a second or two. What makes that hard to time exactly?
solution: People take a fraction of a second to react, which is a big part of a 2-second fall. **Reaction time** is the main source of error. Repeating and averaging, or filming the drop, helps.

prompt: Why do scientific ideas sometimes change over time?

options.text: New evidence is found that the old idea can't explain
Scientists vote to choose the most popular idea
Old ideas are always replaced after 100 years
A famous scientist disagrees, even without evidence

feedback.b: Science isn't decided by a vote. It's decided by evidence.
feedback.c: Ideas that keep matching the evidence can last for a very long time.
feedback.d: Even famous scientists need evidence to change an accepted idea.

hints: What do scientists use to decide whether an idea is right?
solution: Science ideas are based on **evidence**. When new evidence turns up, for example from better equipment, ideas are tested again and may be changed or replaced.

prompt:
The graph shows Mia's results for how long a sugar cube takes to dissolve in water at different temperatures. She did not test 50 °C.

Use the line of best fit to estimate how long a sugar cube would take to dissolve at 50 °C.

hints: Find 50 °C on the x-axis.
Go straight up to the line, then across to the y-axis.
solution: From 50 °C on the x-axis, go up to the line of best fit, then across to the y-axis: about **60 s**. Reading between your measured points like this is called **interpolation**.

prompt:
Hemi wants to find out whether wool or cotton keeps water warmer for longer. He wraps beaker A in wool and fills it with 200 mL of water at 80 °C. He wraps beaker B in cotton and fills it with 100 mL of water at 60 °C. After 20 minutes he measures both temperatures.

Explain why this is **not a fair test**, and describe how Hemi should change his method.
modelAnswer: It isn't a fair test because Hemi changed more than one variable: as well as the material, the volume of water (200 mL vs 100 mL) and the starting temperature (80 °C vs 60 °C) are different. These also affect how fast water cools, so he can't tell whether the material caused any difference. He should use the same volume of water (e.g. 200 mL) and the same starting temperature (e.g. 80 °C) in both beakers, so the only thing that changes is the material. He should measure how much the temperature drops in the same time.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that the volume of water is different
Identifies that the starting temperature is different
Says only the material should change, with the volume and starting temperature kept the same (controlled)

hints: List everything that is different between beaker A and beaker B.
In a fair test, how many of those should be different?
solution: Two extra variables changed: the **volume of water** and the **starting temperature**. To make it fair, keep both the same in each beaker and change **only the material**.

prompt:
Aroha's hypothesis was: "If the ramp is higher, then the toy car will roll further." Her results are:

| Ramp height (cm) | Mean distance rolled (m) |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.8 |
| 20 | 1.4 |
| 30 | 2.0 |
| 40 | 2.5 |
| 50 | 3.1 |

Write a conclusion for her investigation.
modelAnswer: As the height of the ramp increased, the distance the car rolled also increased. At a height of 10 cm the car rolled 0.8 m, but at 50 cm it rolled 3.1 m, nearly four times as far. This supports Aroha's hypothesis that a higher ramp makes the car roll further.

rubric.criterion: Describes the trend: as ramp height increases, the distance rolled increases
Uses data from the table as evidence (e.g. 10 cm → 0.8 m and 50 cm → 3.1 m)
States that the results support the hypothesis

hints: A strong conclusion has three parts: the pattern, some data, and whether the hypothesis was supported.
solution: Trend: higher ramp → further distance. Evidence: 0.8 m at 10 cm up to 3.1 m at 50 cm. This **supports** the hypothesis.

prompt: Ruby grows two groups of bean plants. Group A is in sunlight **and** given fertiliser. Group B is in the shade with **no** fertiliser. After two weeks, group A is taller. Can Ruby conclude that fertiliser makes bean plants grow taller?

options.text: No, because two variables were changed, so she can't tell which one made the difference
Yes, because the plants with fertiliser grew taller
Yes, because she used two groups of plants
No, because bean plants don't need sunlight

feedback.b: The fertilised plants also had more light, so the light could explain the difference.
feedback.c: Using groups is good, but the groups must differ in only one way.
feedback.d: Plants do need light for photosynthesis, which is exactly why light is a problem here.

hints: How many things are different between group A and group B?
solution: **No.** Light and fertiliser were both changed, so the extra growth could be due to either one (or both). For a fair test, both groups should get the same light and only the fertiliser should differ.

prompt: Grace dropped her paper helicopter only **once** for each wing length. Her teacher says her results are not reliable. Why?

options.text: With only one trial, a single mistake (like a slow reaction on the stopwatch) could change a result, and she can't check it
Paper helicopters always fall at exactly the same speed
She should have changed the wing length and the paper at the same time
One trial is more accurate because you don't get tired

feedback.b: Small differences between drops, like reaction time or air movement, mean results vary.
feedback.c: Changing two variables would make it an unfair test.
feedback.d: Repeats help you spot and reduce errors. Being tired isn't the main issue.

hints: How would she know if one of her results was wrong?
solution: With only one result for each wing length, there's no way to spot an error or average it out. **Repeating** each drop (e.g. three times) and finding the mean makes the results more reliable.

prompt: A paper helicopter takes about 1.5 s to fall 2 m, and Noah's timing varies a lot. Which change would **best** reduce the error caused by his reaction time?

options.text: Drop it from a greater height so the fall takes longer, and repeat each drop several times
Use a stopwatch that shows thousandths of a second
Drop it from a lower height so it's easier to watch
Time only one drop so he stays focused

feedback.b: A more precise display doesn't help if Noah's thumb is still about 0.2 s late. The reaction time error stays the same.
feedback.c: A shorter fall makes the reaction time a **bigger** part of the measured time.
feedback.d: One drop gives no way to check or average out errors.

hints: His reaction time is roughly the same however long the fall is.
What happens to the *size* of that error compared with the total time if the fall lasts longer?
solution: Reaction time adds roughly the same error to every measurement. If the fall takes longer, that error is a **smaller fraction** of the total time. Repeating and averaging reduces it further. A more precise stopwatch doesn't fix a human reaction-time error.

prompt:
In 1912, Alfred Wegener suggested that the continents slowly move across the Earth. At first, most scientists rejected his idea. Today the theory of plate tectonics is accepted.

Use this example to explain how scientific ideas are tested and can change over time.
modelAnswer: Wegener had some evidence, such as the way the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together and matching fossils on different continents. Other scientists questioned his idea because he couldn't explain how continents could move, and scientists expect strong evidence before they accept a new idea. Later (in the 1950s and 1960s), new evidence from mapping and measuring the sea floor showed that the sea floor is spreading and the plates move. With this new evidence, scientists changed their thinking, and the idea developed into the theory of plate tectonics. This shows that science ideas are based on evidence and can change when new evidence is found.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the idea was questioned/rejected because there wasn't enough evidence or no explanation of how it worked
States that new evidence was later found (e.g. from studying the sea floor)
Concludes that scientific ideas are based on evidence and change (or develop) when new evidence appears

hints: Why might other scientists not have accepted the idea at first?
What changed between 1912 and today?
solution: Scientists test new ideas against the evidence. Wegener's idea was doubted because it lacked a mechanism. Later evidence from the sea floor supported moving plates, so the idea was accepted and developed. Science changes when the **evidence** changes.

stem:
Sione investigates how the height a tennis ball is dropped from affects how high it bounces. He drops the ball onto the concrete outside the lab, measures each bounce with a metre ruler, and repeats each height three times. His mean results are:

| Drop height (cm) | Mean bounce height (cm) |
|---|---|
| 50 | 28 |
| 100 | 55 |
| 150 | 83 |
| 200 | 110 |
prompt: In Sione's investigation, the independent variable is the [[a]]. The dependent variable is the [[b]]. A controlled variable is the [[c]].
hints: The independent variable is the one Sione chooses and changes on purpose. The dependent variable is the one he measures.
solution: Sione **changes** the drop height (independent), **measures** the bounce height (dependent), and keeps the **same ball** and the same concrete surface (controlled), so the test is fair.

stem:
Sione investigates how the height a tennis ball is dropped from affects how high it bounces. He drops the ball onto the concrete outside the lab, measures each bounce with a metre ruler, and repeats each height three times. His mean results are:

| Drop height (cm) | Mean bounce height (cm) |
|---|---|
| 50 | 28 |
| 100 | 55 |
| 150 | 83 |
| 200 | 110 |
prompt: Write a conclusion for Sione's investigation.
modelAnswer: As the drop height increased, the bounce height also increased. For example, when the ball was dropped from 50 cm it bounced 28 cm, but from 200 cm it bounced 110 cm. The bounce height was always a little more than half of the drop height, so doubling the drop height roughly doubled the bounce height.

rubric.criterion: Describes the trend: as the drop height increases, the bounce height increases
Uses data from the table as evidence, e.g. 50 cm → 28 cm and 200 cm → 110 cm
Describes the pattern more precisely, e.g. the bounce is always just over half the drop height, or doubling the drop height roughly doubles the bounce

hints: Start with the trend: what happens to one variable as the other increases?
Compare each bounce height with its drop height. Is there a simple link?
solution: A full conclusion gives the trend, quotes data, and describes the pattern. Here the bounce height is roughly proportional to the drop height: 28 ÷ 50, 55 ÷ 100, 83 ÷ 150 and 110 ÷ 200 are all about 0.55, so the ball always bounces to just over half the height it was dropped from.

stem:
Sione investigates how the height a tennis ball is dropped from affects how high it bounces. He drops the ball onto the concrete outside the lab, measures each bounce with a metre ruler, and repeats each height three times. His mean results are:

| Drop height (cm) | Mean bounce height (cm) |
|---|---|
| 50 | 28 |
| 100 | 55 |
| 150 | 83 |
| 200 | 110 |
prompt: Sione found it hard to see exactly how high the ball went at the top of each bounce. Which change would make each bounce measurement more **accurate**?

options.text: Film each bounce in front of the metre ruler and replay it in slow motion
Test more drop heights, such as 250 cm and 300 cm
Use a heavier ball, so that it bounces more slowly
Do only one drop at each height, so he can concentrate

feedback.b: More drop heights give more data points, but each bounce would still be just as hard to read.
feedback.c: Changing the ball changes a controlled variable, so it becomes a different experiment. It doesn't fix the reading problem.
feedback.d: Fewer trials make results less reliable, and they don't make each reading any clearer.

hints: The problem is that the top of each bounce only lasts a split second.
solution: The top of a bounce happens in a split second, so it is easy to misjudge. A **slow-motion video** in front of the ruler lets Sione pause at the highest point and read it carefully, so each measurement is more accurate.

stem: Aroha investigates how the length of a pendulum affects the time it takes to swing. She ties a metal nut to a piece of string, pulls it to one side and lets it go. For each length, she times **10** complete swings.
prompt: Which of these should Aroha keep the same, so that her test is fair? Select **all** that apply.

options.text: The mass of the nut on the end of the string
How far she pulls the nut to the side before letting it go
The type of string
The number of swings she times
The length of the string
The time for 10 swings

hints: Anything that could affect the result, apart from the length, should be kept the same.
solution: Controlled variables: the mass of the nut, how far it is pulled back, the type of string and the number of swings timed. The **length** is the independent variable (what she changes), and the **time for 10 swings** is the dependent variable (what she measures).

stem: Aroha investigates how the length of a pendulum affects the time it takes to swing. She ties a metal nut to a piece of string, pulls it to one side and lets it go. For each length, she times **10** complete swings.
prompt: Aroha's results are shown on the graph, with a line of best fit. Use the line to estimate the time for 10 swings of a pendulum that is 50 cm long.

Results are plotted at 20 cm (9.0 s), 40 cm (12.7 s), 60 cm (15.5 s), 80 cm (17.9 s) and 100 cm (20.1 s). A smooth curve of best fit starts at the origin and passes through the points, getting less steep as the length increases.

modelAnswer: As the length of the pendulum increases, the time for 10 swings increases. But the line of best fit is a curve that gets less steep: each extra 20 cm adds less time than the one before (from 20 cm to 40 cm the time goes up by about 3.7 s, but from 80 cm to 100 cm it only goes up by about 2.2 s). So the time is not directly proportional to the length. For example, doubling the length from 50 cm to 100 cm does not double the time (about 14 s to about 20 s).

rubric.criterion: States the trend: as the length increases, the time for 10 swings increases
Describes the curve: the increase gets smaller / the graph gets less steep / time is not directly proportional to length (ideally with data)

hints: Is the line of best fit straight, or does it curve? What does that tell you?
solution: Longer pendulums take longer to swing, but the curve flattens out, so each extra centimetre of length adds a little less time. A straight line through the origin would have meant the time was directly proportional to the length, and this graph isn't.

stem:
Ella tests four brands of paper towel to find out which one absorbs the most water. She cuts a 10 cm × 10 cm square of each towel, dips it in water for 10 seconds, lets it drip for 5 seconds, then squeezes the water out into a measuring cylinder. She does three trials for each brand.

| Brand | Trial 1 (mL) | Trial 2 (mL) | Trial 3 (mL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 9 | 7 |
| B | 15 | 16 | 15 |
| C | 6 | 13 | 7 |
| D | 10 | 10 | 11 |
prompt: Which result is most likely an **outlier**?

options.text: Brand C, trial 2 (13 mL)
Brand B, trial 2 (16 mL)
Brand C, trial 1 (6 mL)
Brand D, trial 3 (11 mL)

feedback.b: 16 mL is the biggest number in the table, but it fits well with Brand B's other results (15 and 15). An outlier doesn't fit the pattern of its **own** trials.
feedback.c: 6 mL is the smallest number in the table, but it is close to Brand C's other normal result (7 mL).
feedback.d: 11 mL is only 1 mL away from 10 mL. Small differences between trials are normal.

hints: Compare each result with the other two trials for the same brand.
solution: Brand C's results are 6, 13 and 7 mL. The 13 mL result is about twice the others, so it doesn't fit the pattern: it is an **outlier**, probably caused by a mistake. It should be checked or repeated, and left out of the mean.

stem:
Ella tests four brands of paper towel to find out which one absorbs the most water. She cuts a 10 cm × 10 cm square of each towel, dips it in water for 10 seconds, lets it drip for 5 seconds, then squeezes the water out into a measuring cylinder. She does three trials for each brand.

| Brand | Trial 1 (mL) | Trial 2 (mL) | Trial 3 (mL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 9 | 7 |
| B | 15 | 16 | 15 |
| C | 6 | 13 | 7 |
| D | 10 | 10 | 11 |
prompt: Why did Ella cut every paper towel into a square of the same size?

options.text: So the size of the towel is controlled, making it a fair test
So that the squares fit inside the measuring cylinder
So she could measure the size as the dependent variable
Because the size of the towel is her independent variable

feedback.b: The towels are squeezed out over the cylinder; they don't have to fit inside it. The real reason is fairness.
feedback.c: The size isn't measured as a result. It is kept the same so it can't affect the result.
feedback.d: Her independent variable is the **brand** of paper towel. The size is kept the same.

hints: A bigger piece of towel could soak up more water, whatever the brand is.
solution: A bigger piece would absorb more water whatever its brand. Keeping the size the same (a **controlled variable**) means only the brand changes, so it is a fair test.

stem:
Ella tests four brands of paper towel to find out which one absorbs the most water. She cuts a 10 cm × 10 cm square of each towel, dips it in water for 10 seconds, lets it drip for 5 seconds, then squeezes the water out into a measuring cylinder. She does three trials for each brand.

| Brand | Trial 1 (mL) | Trial 2 (mL) | Trial 3 (mL) |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 8 | 9 | 7 |
| B | 15 | 16 | 15 |
| C | 6 | 13 | 7 |
| D | 10 | 10 | 11 |
prompt: Calculate the mean volume of water absorbed by Brand C, leaving out the outlier.
hints: Find the result that does not fit the pattern for Brand C and leave it out.
Add the other two results and divide by 2.
solution: Leave out the outlier (13 mL). Mean $= \dfrac{6 + 7}{2} = \dfrac{13}{2} =$ **6.5 mL**. (Including the outlier would give $26 \div 3 \approx 8.7$ mL, which makes Brand C look better than it really is.)

prompt: When you draw a line graph of your results, which axis should the **independent** variable go on?

options.text: The horizontal axis (x-axis)
The vertical axis (y-axis)
Whichever axis has the bigger numbers
It doesn't need to go on an axis

feedback.b: The vertical (y) axis is for the dependent variable, the one you measure.
feedback.c: The size of the numbers doesn't matter. The independent variable always goes on the x-axis.
feedback.d: Both variables need an axis, so you can plot the points.

hints: The variable you change goes 'across'.
solution: The **independent variable** (what you change) goes along the **x-axis**, and the dependent variable (what you measure) goes up the y-axis.

prompt: What do we call the average you get by adding up a set of results and dividing by how many results there are?
hints: It is the kind of average used in most science results tables.
solution: This is the **mean**. For example, the mean of 4, 5 and 6 is $(4 + 5 + 6) \div 3 = 5$.

prompt: In a results table, where should the units go?

options.text: In the column headings, e.g. Time (s)
After every number in the table
In a sentence underneath the table
Units aren't needed in a table

feedback.b: Writing units after every number clutters the table. Put them once, in the heading.
feedback.c: Units belong with the column they describe, in the heading.
feedback.d: Without units, nobody knows whether '20' means 20 seconds or 20 minutes.

hints: Units only need to be written once for each column.
solution: Units go in the **column headings**, like 'Time (s)' or 'Temperature (°C)'. Then the numbers in the table don't need units after them.

prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

right.text: Similar results are obtained when the test is repeated
A result that doesn't fit the pattern
Something that makes results less accurate, e.g. reaction time
A statement that answers the question using the evidence

hints: 'Reliable' is about repeating a test; 'accurate' is about the true value.
solution: Reliable → repeats agree. Accurate → close to the true value. Outlier → doesn't fit the pattern. Source of error → something that makes results less accurate. Conclusion → answers the question using the evidence.

prompt: Kiri investigates how the temperature of water affects the time it takes for jelly crystals to dissolve. She tests 20 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C and 80 °C. What type of graph should she draw?

options.text: A line graph, because both variables are numbers
A bar graph, because she only tested four temperatures
A pie graph, because the times add up to a total
A bar graph, because time is the dependent variable

feedback.b: The number of tests doesn't decide the graph type. Temperature is a number that can take any value, so a line graph shows the trend between the points.
feedback.c: Pie graphs show the parts of a whole. These times don't make up a whole.
feedback.d: Bar graphs are used when the **independent** variable is in categories (like brands), not numbers.

hints: Is the independent variable a category (like a brand) or a number?
solution: Both variables are numbers that can take any value, so Kiri should draw a **line graph** with a line of best fit. Use a bar graph when the independent variable is a category, such as brand or material.

prompt: At the school athletics day, three timekeepers time the winner of the 100 m sprint. Their times are 14.2 s, 14.5 s and 14.3 s. What is the mean time? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Add the three times together.
Divide the total by 3, then round to 1 decimal place.
solution: $14.2 + 14.5 + 14.3 = 43.0$ s, and $43.0 \div 3 = 14.33...$, which is **14.3 s** to 1 decimal place. Using three timekeepers and taking the mean makes the result more reliable than trusting one stopwatch.

prompt: Why do scientists publish their methods and results, for example in science journals?

options.text: So other scientists can check the work and try to repeat the experiments
So that an idea becomes true once it has been printed
So that no other scientist is allowed to study the same topic
So that scientists can vote on which idea they like best

feedback.b: Publishing doesn't make an idea true. Ideas are accepted when lots of evidence supports them.
feedback.c: Publishing invites other scientists to study and test the same topic.
feedback.d: Science ideas are judged on evidence, not on a vote or on popularity.

hints: How can anyone else be sure that an experiment's results are right?
solution: Sharing methods and results lets other scientists **check and repeat** the work. If they get the same results, the evidence gets stronger. If they don't, the idea may need to change.

prompt:
Mateo wants to investigate this question: *How does the steepness of a ramp affect the time it takes a marble to roll down it?*

Write a hypothesis for his investigation.
modelAnswer: If the ramp is steeper, then the marble will take less time to roll down it, because gravity pulls it down a steeper slope more strongly, so it speeds up more quickly.

rubric.criterion: Makes a testable prediction linking the two variables (e.g. if the ramp is steeper, then the time will be shorter)
Gives a scientific reason (e.g. because gravity pulls it down a steeper slope more strongly, so it speeds up more)

hints: Use the pattern: If… then… because…
solution: A hypothesis is a **testable prediction with a reason**. It says how the dependent variable (time) will change when the independent variable (steepness) changes, and why. It doesn't matter if the results later show that it was wrong.

prompt: A good line graph has the [[a]] variable on the x-axis, axis labels that include the [[b]], and a smooth line of [[c]] instead of lines that join one dot to the next.
hints: The variable you change goes along the bottom.
How would a reader know whether the numbers are in seconds or minutes?
solution: **Independent** variable on the x-axis; axis labels with **units**, e.g. 'Time (s)'; and a smooth line of **best fit** that shows the trend without being thrown off by small errors.

prompt: Mia and Tom each drop the same paper helicopter three times from 2 m. Mia's times are 2.1 s, 2.3 s and 2.2 s. Tom's times are 1.5 s, 2.9 s and 2.2 s. Whose results are more **reliable**?

options.text: Mia's, because her three times are close together
Tom's, because his results cover a wider range
They are equally reliable, because both means are 2.2 s
Tom's, because one of his times is exactly the mean

feedback.b: A wide spread means the results don't agree with each other, which makes them less reliable.
feedback.c: The means are the same, but Tom's individual results are much more spread out, so they are less consistent.
feedback.d: One result matching the mean doesn't make a set of results reliable. Look at how much the times vary.

hints: Reliable results are consistent: they agree with each other when the test is repeated.
solution: Mia's results only vary by 0.2 s, while Tom's vary by 1.4 s. Mia's results are consistent when repeated, so they are **more reliable**, even though both means are 2.2 s.

prompt: Ari wants to find the thickness of one page of his science book. Why is it better to measure the thickness of 100 pages with a ruler and divide by 100?

options.text: One page is too thin to measure with a ruler, but 100 pages can be measured accurately
Every page is a different thickness, so he needs to find the thickest page
It is quicker to measure 100 pages than to measure one page
A ruler can't measure anything thinner than 1 cm

feedback.b: Dividing by 100 gives the average thickness of a page, not the thickest one.
feedback.c: Speed isn't the point; accuracy is. The smallest marks on a ruler (1 mm) are much bigger than the thickness of one page.
feedback.d: A ruler has 1 mm marks, but one page is only about 0.1 mm thick, so it still can't be measured accurately on its own.

hints: The smallest marks on a ruler are 1 mm apart. How thick is one page?
solution: A page is about 0.1 mm thick, much smaller than the 1 mm marks on a ruler. A stack of 100 pages is about 10 mm thick, which a ruler can measure well, and any reading error is shared out over 100 pages. Timing 10 swings of a pendulum instead of one uses the same idea.

prompt: Plan a fair test to find out whether the type of surface (carpet, wood or concrete) affects how far a toy car rolls after it leaves a ramp. In your plan, name the independent, dependent and controlled variables, and say how you will make your results reliable.
modelAnswer:
Independent variable: the type of surface the car rolls onto (carpet, wood, concrete).
Dependent variable: the distance the car rolls from the bottom of the ramp, measured with a tape measure.
Controlled variables: the same toy car, the same ramp at the same height, and releasing the car from the same starting line without pushing it.
Reliability: do three runs on each surface, check for outliers and calculate the mean distance for each surface.

rubric.criterion: Independent variable: the type of surface
Dependent variable: the distance rolled, with how it is measured (e.g. tape measure)
At least two sensible controlled variables (e.g. same car, same ramp height, same release point, no push)
Repeats each surface (e.g. 3 times) and calculates a mean

hints: Start with what you change, what you measure, and what you keep the same.
How many times will you test each surface?
solution: A fair test changes only the surface, measures the distance rolled, keeps everything else the same, and repeats each test so a mean can be calculated.

prompt: Pita measures the temperature of a cup of hot water every minute for 10 minutes, using a thermometer and a stopwatch. Identify **one** source of error in his method, and suggest how he could reduce it.
modelAnswer: One source of error is reading the thermometer from above or below instead of at eye level, which gives a wrong reading. He could make sure his eye is level with the top of the liquid in the thermometer, or use a digital temperature probe (data logger), which records the temperature automatically every minute.

rubric.criterion: A valid source of error, e.g. reading the thermometer at an angle, not reading exactly on each minute, the thermometer touching the cup, draughts or changes in room temperature
A matching improvement that would reduce that error, e.g. read at eye level, use a data logger or temperature probe, keep the bulb in the middle of the water, do it away from windows

hints: Think about how Pita reads the thermometer, and how he times each reading.
solution: Any sensible source of error is fine, as long as the improvement matches it and would actually reduce that error.

prompt: Ruby's results support her hypothesis. Her friend says, "So you've proved that your hypothesis is true." Which reply is the most scientific?

options.text: The results support it, but more tests might show otherwise, so it isn't proved
Yes, one investigation that agrees with a hypothesis proves it
No, a hypothesis can only be proved by a famous scientist
Yes, because she got the result she expected

feedback.b: One set of results is evidence, not proof. Other tests, or other conditions, could give different results.
feedback.c: Science doesn't depend on who you are. Ideas are judged on evidence that anyone can check.
feedback.d: Getting the result you expected supports a hypothesis, but scientists stay open to new evidence.

hints: Could a future investigation ever find something different?
solution: In science, evidence can **support** an idea, but never prove it for certain. Other scientists might repeat the test, or test new conditions, and find something different. That is why science ideas can change over time.

prompt: Hōhepa tests how much fertiliser makes pea plants grow tallest. He tests 0 g, 2 g, 4 g and 6 g, and the plants are taller each time. Why can't he be sure that 20 g would grow even taller plants?

options.text: 20 g is far outside the range he tested, and the pattern might change there
He can be sure, because a pattern always continues in the same way
He would need to draw a bar graph before he could predict anything
Because fertiliser stops working at exactly 6 g

feedback.b: Patterns don't always continue. He only has evidence inside the range he tested.
feedback.c: The type of graph doesn't change what the evidence shows (and this data needs a line graph anyway).
feedback.d: He has no evidence about what happens above 6 g. The pattern could change at any point.

hints: What evidence does he have about amounts bigger than 6 g?
solution: Results only give good evidence **within the range tested**. Predicting far beyond it is risky, because the pattern may change. In real life, too much fertiliser can damage plant roots. Hōhepa would need to test bigger amounts to find out.

prompt: Scientists want to find out whether a new treatment protects kauri trees from kauri dieback disease. Describe how they could design a fair and reliable test, and explain why each feature is needed.
modelAnswer: They should treat one group of kauri trees and leave a similar group untreated as a comparison (a control group). Then any difference in health between the two groups can be linked to the treatment, not to something else. They should use lots of trees in each group, because individual trees vary and some might stay healthy (or get sick) by chance; a large sample gives more reliable results. They should also keep other variables the same, for example by choosing trees of a similar size and age, in the same area with the same soil, and checking them in the same way over the same length of time.

rubric.criterion: Includes an untreated (control) group to compare with, so any difference can be linked to the treatment
Uses many trees in each group, because trees vary and a large sample reduces the effect of chance (more reliable)
Keeps other variables the same, e.g. similar size or age of trees, same area or soil, same time period

hints: How would the scientists know whether a healthy tree was healthy because of the treatment?
Would testing just one or two trees be enough?
solution: A strong design has a control group for comparison, a large number of trees for reliability, and controlled variables so that the treatment is the only difference between the groups.
